utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Margetts, are you ready to continue the examination in chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's my first question. Then the usher is invited to escort Mr. Djokanovic into the courtroom. Mr. Harmon, has any solution been found for the beginning of next week?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have instructed staff to contact potential witnesses. We have done so. I'm going to get a report this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I take it that the Defence will be informed?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: As soon as I get confirmation from the witnesses, then I will inform the Defence immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we're waiting for the witness to come into court, I would just like to place on the record my gratitude to Mr. Sam Lowery from the office of legal aid in the registry. He was able to assist us with finding an interpreter yesterday evening at 6.00. Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that it will be highly appreciated that you express your -- that you express your gratitude in this way.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djokanovic, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated. I'd like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I give Mr. Margetts the opportunity to continue your examination, I'd like to ask you to slow down the speed of your speech because the interpreters and whatever you say has to be translated into English and into French. The interpreters really have difficulties in keeping at your pace. Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. Margetts: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, before the court went into recess yesterday afternoon, we were looking at some transcripts of conversations that you had with Dr. Radovan Karadzic and I'd like to resume this morning referring to those transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, could the witness please be shown Exhibit P548A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's the transcript of a conversation held on the 29th of December and it has the internal number CD-41-28-11/02/051. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, at the commencement of this conversation, you report to Dr. Karadzic in respect of events that are taking place. In particular, I'd like to refer you to the section of the conversation where you say more than 40 parties. Karadzic responds, "More than 40." And you say, "And Vojo reported his guerilla fighters" and Karadzic says "Who, Seselj?" And you say, "uh-huh". Could you explain to the Court what it is you're referring to in that passage?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This talk was between Dr. Karadzic and myself. On the eve of the convention on Yugoslavia, on the 26th of December, 1991, there was a meeting at the SFRY Presidency attended by parties from Bosnia and Herzegovina. At that meeting, we agreed to establish a coordinating body and prepare the convention on Yugoslavia in the federal Assembly which would be attended by all interested parties from all the Yugoslav republics. That was actually the subject of this conversation between Dr. Karadzic and me as they had told us from Belgrade where the secretariat of the coordinating body was that 40 parties had responded to confirm their attendance at the convention for Yugoslavia and as Dr. Seselj had confirmed the attendance of his party, I told Karadzic about that being interested to hear his reaction to that all. That is -- and he understood when I said that Vojo had reported his guerilla fighters. At that time they had two wings, Seselj's party; one was the political party and the other was the Chetnik movement. So I asked Dr. Karadzic -- I told Dr. Karadzic about this, wanted to hear what his reaction would be and he just told to me, "Who Seselj?", without any further comments. He then passed on to another subject. He told me that he had talked with Micunovic who was the president of the democratic party at the time. Also regarding their participation in the convention on Yugoslavia and we agreed that I should send an official fax to the president of the democratic party, Mr. Micunovic so that the democratic party would also attend that meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, it's now well known that Vojislav Seselj's party recruited volunteers who fought in the wars in Croatia and in Bosnia, in particular at the end of 1991 --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to evidence being given via a question, Your Honour. In my submission, that's inappropriate and I would object to questioning of that nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, at least the question is not -- I don't know what the question is but if it would be about what you put to the witness, then it certainly is leading and not a bit, but entirely leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will withdraw the question and the reason for the comment was really that this matter does have quite a deal of notoriety these days, but I will put the question in a non-leading form.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, are you aware whether or not Vojislav Seselj recruited volunteers for the purpose of them fighting in the conflicts in the region toward the end of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, that's leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is leading to some extent. Let me take it over. Dr. Djokanovic, what could you tell us about the activities of Vojislav Seselj? At that time, what were his main activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regards the activities of Mr. Seselj, I can only tell you about what I saw on television or read in the papers. I do not know Mr. Seselj. It was on the 3rd of January at this convention that I saw him for the first time which he attended with his delegation. I know from the papers that he organised people to go and fight as volunteers in the war theatres in Croatia and later in Bosnia. So knowing that he was sending volunteers to Croatia, I asked Karadzic about it so that we would adopt some sort of a position because he was also a member of the coordinating body for the convention on Yugoslavia which I was a member and I wanted to see what position we would adopt as regards Seselj. So when the convention was taking place in the Assembly conference room, we saw that Seselj had sat with his people in the second row and they asked me, Dr. Djokanovic, he has sat in the second row, what should we do about it? And I said to them, he has a registered party in Serbia, he has come here with his representatives of his party. He has the right to sit where he pleases. We have not numbered the seats so everyone can sit where they please. In a word, we did not have any special or differentiated political posture in regard to Dr. Seselj or his political party or the wing of the party which was questionable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you when you said in this telephone conversation and for your report, "his guerilla fighters," were you referring to persons recruited by Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but did you take that from the media or were you informed otherwise about Seselj reporting guerilla fighters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Solely from the media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, in the course of the answers to the previous questions, you've referred to the Convention on Yugoslavia. During January and February of 1992, were you active in Belgrade in convening the Convention on Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After this meeting was held in the Presidency of the SFRY on the 26th of January, 1991, this coordinating body was set up comprising the presidents of parties from Bosnia and Herzegovina and I headed this coordinating body. We also agreed to establish an administrative secretariat and the federal state offered its good offices for that purpose, namely an office, a certain number of telephone numbers, and a person to mind the phones. During those five or six days, I would go to Belgrade to see -- I went to Belgrade to see how things were unfolding and then on the 2nd of January, 1992, all of us together from Bosnia and Herzegovina went to Belgrade to attend the convention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's a reference in this answer to the date January 1991 at line 16. If I could just clarify that with the witness. Dr. Djokanovic, what was the date of the SFRY Presidency session that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 2nd of January, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the period January and February 1992 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, the matter has not been -- you mentioned two dates, the first when the meeting was held in the Presidency of the SFRY, when the coordinating body was set up comprising the presidents of the parties. The second date you mentioned was the 2nd of January when all of you together from Bosnia went to Belgrade. Now, that first date when the meeting in the Presidency was held when the coordinating body was set up, what was that date, because you mentioned the 26th of January, 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the 26th of December, 1991 after that meeting, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That clarifies the issue. Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, could you tell the Court where you were in January and February 1992, that is, during which period were you in Belgrade and which period were you in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the convention was over, I returned to Sarajevo and on -- then I went to Belgrade on a couple of occasions to attend sessions of the federal chamber, or rather, the committee that was preparing the text of the convention on Yugoslavia. So after the convention, the meeting was held, apart from the Bosnia and Herzegovina parties that attended the meeting, on the 2nd of January, 1992, that is, there were also parties from Serbia, Montenegro, Macedonia and Croatia. There were over 100 participants there. When I say 100 participants, I am talking about organisations, I'm not quite sure what the number of the signatories to that convention on Yugoslavia was. The conclusions of the convention was that the federal Assembly should adopt a comprehensive piece of legislation to address, or rather, to resolve the political crisis in the SFRY. One of the committees of the federal chamber was entrusted with a task of preparing the text of a law to comprehensively address the Yugoslav crisis. So it was for that matter that I went to Belgrade on a number of occasions. I don't remember exactly how many. Then we had another meeting on the 14th of February, 1992. This time the meeting was attended only by those who had signed the convention text, the convention from the beginning of January 1992, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, thank you for that explanation. Now, moving to March 1992 -- Your Honour, if the witness could be presented with the -- not the next two exhibits, we will skip those, but we'll move to the Assembly sessions which are marked numbers 25, 26, and 27 in the list of exhibits and have previously been presented through the witness Treanor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you provided copies to the registry or ... the 25th might have been distributed already because I remember that you already started.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, these are bulky documents and copies in the normal number have not been prepared. These documents are in the binders with registry and if the document could be presented on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, they could be, but would it not have -- have you informed the registrar on what documents to find in advance of this session? I mean now we start looking for them whereas I certainly know that Ms. Philpott would have looked to find them. I do understand that you have informed Ms. Philpott but there's not a spare copy for the witness at this point so ... It should be clear from the beginning whether you find them in your binders and present them to the witness or whether the registry is supposed to find them in order to save time in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could assist the case manager, if we could just have a short pause while I do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a kind of race to see who finds them first. The registry won. Can we have the English version on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, the pages that we would need to display on the ELMO are from page 12 of the translation. Your Honour, the portions of the English text that I'm referring to are the speeches of Mr. Krajisnik which commences on page 12 and the speech of Dr. Djokanovic which follows the speech of Mr. Krajisnik and commences on page 14 and runs through to page 15.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, you have before you the Assembly session from 18 March 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, did you attend the Assembly of the Serbian People on 18 March 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, if you could open up the Assembly session and you could refer to pages 14 where a speech of Momcilo Krajisnik commences, and if you could read the text through to page 17 where Mr. Krajisnik concludes and then your speech commences. And then read your speech through to nearly the end of page 18. That's in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I just inquire whether or not you have a copy of these pages?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, we are reading from the -- of course there is one copy in the hands of the registry but I mean that's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm informed by the case manager that we have nine copies of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine, we spent already three minutes on getting the right material on the ELMO and I do understand now that we are going to spend another three minutes on distributing nine copies available. I mean let's get practical, Mr. Margetts. And if I just may say in relation to that, if you have already announced that you are going to pay attention to the speech delivered by Mr. Djokanovic, the next question whether he was present on not sounds a bit -- of course it's all within the realm of advocacy but it's not very practical advocacy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for that guidance. In the realm of being practical, Your Honour, if I could respectively suggest that it may be more convenient if the transcripts that we have here were provided to you, it would be quicker, I suggest, than the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, no one opposed against them to be distributed five minutes ago, would they? If I sound a bit irritated, I promise you that I'll suppress that but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course I'm suppressing the same irritation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do we start on page 14, Mr. Margetts?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you could start on page 12 and read through to page 15.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, do you recall making the speech that commences on page 16 of your copy?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: March was a very significant month, I recall very vividly the Assembly sessions and the speeches by the then most significant politicians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, I'd like to refer you to the first paragraph of your speech where you say that war or peace was discussed and common sense prevailed. Could you explain to the Court what you meant when you made those remarks?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I indicated something along those lines in answer to the question by His Honour. Now this establishment of the Assembly of the Serbian people came several days after the adoption of the memorandum on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina that had been adopted by this unprincipled parliamentary majority. I say unprincipled although it was a majority, but I say unprincipled because it was a coalition of the three parties where two parties chucked the third party and then adopted a memorandum that was against the will of the third party. I said yesterday that there was a euphoria on the side of the SDA and the HDZ whereas on the side of the SDS, their politicians and supporters, there was rage. And at the inaugural session of the Assembly of the Serbian people, there were discussions to the effect that we should start waging a war because people were enraged. However, most of those who took the floor were in favour of resolving the political crisis peacefully, through peaceful means and that we had enough capable people, human resources, to find a solution, find an exit out of this complicated situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, I'll now refer you to further on in your speech, in fact, the second last paragraph of your speech. And in this passage, you state, that you'd like to make a point here and you say, "What has happened to even the highest ranking officials of the Serbs in BH, among them, the president of the Assembly of the Serbian people of BH, that they say publicly, that Yugoslavia does not exist anymore." What were the implications of saying that Yugoslavia did not exist Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. anymore?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the second last passage, I said that I supported the efforts invested by those participating in the negotiations and that success was looming in this negotiation process for the Serbian people. And when I say for the Serbian people, I mean that there was going to be a solution that was going to be acceptable for all the three peoples which would mean success for the Serbian people because we asked no more, no less than the other two peoples. However, during those days, some statements were published in the mass media and I did turn to that when Mr. Krajisnik said that there was no -- that Yugoslavia was no more, I said that none of the politicians could afford to state such a thing because we had to draw our force from the results of the plebescite of the Serbian people held at the end of 1991, where the Serbs had called on all the members of other ethnicities, religions to vote for staying within this country that we loved. So if anyone was to breakup Yugoslavia, that should not be the Serb politicians, because their own people state that they wanted to remain within Yugoslavia. Now you have a conference on Bosnia and Herzegovina, you should focus on the conference and seek for a righteous way out of this problem. That was my message to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the context of the speech that you made, your reference to the fact that is said by high officials that Yugoslavia did not exist anymore, what did you think the implications of that statement were?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that question has been asked and answered in relation to what the implications of saying that Yugoslavia did not exist anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the question was certainly asked. It was my impression that it hadn't been fully answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You get one opportunity to find further clarification of the answer and to see whether it really answered your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, in your view, as soon as it was accepted that Yugoslavia did not exist anymore, what would follow?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the Serb politicians were to accept that Yugoslavia was no more then they did not have any basis for remaining on the political scene because the future Serbian republic and its constitution relied upon the vote of the Serbian people and other people who -- voting in favour of staying within Yugoslavia. The turnout at this particular vote was by far larger than ever before, at least as regards the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that the Serb politicians had no basis for remaining on the political scene, what, then, were the options for the Serb politicians?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were walking out of the Assembly, even though this parliamentary majority that was formed was unprincipled, it was a majority after all. The SDA and the HDZ also had some sort of a logical basis, foundation for saying that they were a parliamentary majority. This was just one political option that was against it. Why should a political option seem to represent the entire peoples. We are walking out of the Assembly, we are establishing an Assembly of the Serbian people which undoubtedly enjoys the support of the Serbian people. Then we establish the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina but that was the maximum that we could do once we got separated from the Bosnian Assembly. We had to walk all the way in order for us to return to normal, to functioning normally once the other side, in future, realises what it had done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, at the commencement of your speech, you referred at -- you referred to the war option. Was war an option for the politicians?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Again, Your Honours, in relation to that question, the question of what Mr. Djokanovic meant about that particular aspect of his speech has already been asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where do we exactly find an answer to this question, Ms. Loukas?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was in relation to -- right at the beginning. I might just check here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was whether the war was an option for politicians.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I'm referring to the question that Mr. Margetts asked of the witness to that portion of his speech and the question is not merely was war an option of the politicians but it actually refers to Mr. Djokanovic's speech and Mr. Djokanovic's speech, Mr. Margetts has asked about in reference to that first paragraph that refers to war and peace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, was war an option for the Serbian politicians?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In grave political crisis, a war is always an option, not only in the -- in this region but of course the politicians do their best to avoid a war. I'm referring, again, to Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Assembly of the Serbian People. Some of the deputies there were hot tempered, blew their fuses easily and wanted to solve the political crisis radically, but I said that most of the deputies in the parliament were for a peaceful solution despite the gravity of the political situation to look for a just and peaceful solution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On 18 March 1992, which politicians made speeches that suggested they wished to solve the crisis radically?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall at this time the names of these people. I do see images of some people who were radical in their speeches in the Assembly in general, but I can't really claim with certainty that they were the ones who spoke that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, just prior to you making your speech where you referred to the war option, you refer to statements about Yugoslavia no longer existing. Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik made a speech and this is what he said. He said, "What is the problem?" He said, "I think the problem is that they want Bosnia and Hercegovina to be internationally recognised at any cost. They want it to be a state. In this respect, it would be good if we could do one thing for strategic reasons, if we could start implementing what we have agreed upon, the ethnic division on the ground, that we start determining the territory, and once the territory is determined, it remains to be established in additional negotiations whose authorities are to function and in what way." Do you recall Mr. Krajisnik making those comments on the 18th of March, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was stated by Mr. Krajisnik on the 18th of March that year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you consider that those comments were consistent with opting for the war option?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is classic leading and I object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I consider that question to not be a leading question. The fact is that the witness will be able to say what he considered those comments consistent with and clearly the topic that we're discussing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but, of course, you're already suggesting with what the consistency would be. If you would have asked whether this would be consistent with any view expressed during that day, then it would have been far less leading. Could you give your comment on this speech, Mr. Djokanovic, where you situate this speech in the, I would say, in the spectrum of political views presented during that meeting and other meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I looked upon the conference on Bosnia and Herzegovina in a positive light not because I was convinced that all the three sides were to reach a just solution, but I was reassured by the fact that the International Community got involved in the resolution of the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina and this body was headed by the Portuguese diplomat Jose Cutileiro. This was reassuring to me because I saw the three sides starting -- entering into negotiations and I hoped that they would come out of the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djokanovic, that's not an answer to my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm coming to that part now. There was, of course, no need to go against the agreed principles and the conference that was scheduled. Why should we talk about ethnic divisions on the ground at the Assembly session in this context, because if this had not been agreed at the earlier session, and it was not, then these are merely speeches contributing to the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just see whether I understand your answer. You said there was no need to go against the agreed principles and the conference that was scheduled. Do I understand that to be that there was no need to go against a solution by negotiations? And then you said, "Why should we talk about ethnic division on the ground at the Assembly session in this context, because if this had not been agreed at the earlier session, and it was not, then these are merely speeches contributing to the war." Do I understand your answer to be that this part of the speech of Mr. Krajisnik, as you said it, was contributing to war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so, Your Honour. If -- but there is one sentence at the beginning which says, "We have agreed."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Where he says, "If we could start implementing what we have agreed upon ..." And then you view the ethnic division was not something that was agreed upon, you suggest that it was and -- advocates to implement that and you say that contributes to war. If I'm misunderstanding you, please tell me, but ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the sentence needs to be reread. If you will allow me, I will reread it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "In this sense, it would strategically be good to do one thing, to start with what we had agreed upon, ethnic divisions on the ground. If at the conference on Bosnia and Herzegovina, the three ruling sides had agreed to divide along the ethnic lines and had this been agreed as in a position of the International Community, then this would have been a totally different matter."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that raises the question what actually was meant by "we". If we could start implementing what "we" have agreed upon. Do I understand your answer to be that this was at least not an agreement between the three parties involved. Would you consider it a possibility to understand the "we" for "we Serbs"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until this Assembly session, I had attended all the previous Assembly sessions and not at a single one had we reached such an agreement. As a matter of fact, this topic was not discussed at all, so my dilemma was who are the "we" in these sides, the parties that were involved in this agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear. Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, I'd now like to move to another Assembly session from March 1992, and that is the 10th Assembly session that was held on the 11th of March, 1992. Dr. Djokanovic, were you in attendance at the session on 11 March, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we have another nine copies or ...

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you tell me that I delivered a speech at this Assembly session, I will have to say that I was present at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't have the copies of this Assembly session. For the purposes of this session, it will be adequate for one of the pages to be displayed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, what page should that be?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And that should be page ERN 0083-6985.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm just wondering what page that is in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: In the B/C/S, it is ERN 0081-6436 through to 6437.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm much obliged. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, in answer to your question, I haven't found your name in the list of attendees at this session but I think after we've discussed the speech here, you may recall whether or not you were present when this speech was made. I refer you to the speech of Dr. Radovan Karadzic which followed comments from Momcilo Krajisnik when he opened the session. And that speech commences on page 0081-6436 on the version for you and continues over on to page 0081-6437. And the comments I'm interested in, and I invite your comment on, are the comments in the second paragraph which is at the bottom of the first page and the top of the second page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Dr. Djokanovic, the comments that I'm referring to are the following and that is, Karadzic states, "Fortunately, you realise that a conference on Bosnia and Herzegovina was what was needed and that nothing done against the will of one ethnic community could succeed in Bosnia, that such action could lead only to uncontrolled processes and chaos, the result of which would be a bloody civil war, with hundreds of thousands dead and hundreds of destroyed cities, after which what we would have is the same situation as we have now with three --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, could you mind your speed of speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: "We have with three Bosnian and Hercegovinas, but only after a war, and with much less population in cities, which would be completely ethnically homogenous. For it must be assumed that the forcible and bloody removal of minority peoples from one region to another would be carried out on a large scale in a civil war." Dr. Djokanovic, was Dr. Karadzic's characterisation of what a war in Bosnia would entail your understanding of what a war in Bosnia would entail?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. In fact, in the press article for Sarajevo Oslobodjenje which I referred to yesterday, I said that if there was a war, it would be one of the most disastrous, religious wars unprecedented in the theretofore history.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it your understanding, therefore, that when any politician opted for the war option, they were opting for the forcible removal of ethnic groups from areas?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Again, this question is entirely objectionable and entirely leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, the objection is sustained. Would you please rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, when any politician in Bosnia opted for the war option, can you characterise what type of war you thought they were opting for?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, a question of that nature is very unlikely to be helpful to the Trial Chamber phrased as it is: "Any politician." It's in my view a speculative question that would be of very little assistance to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have heard evidence that politicians were opting for war although there was a larger number which would try to find other solutions. I do understand the question to be a reference to those who opted for war. What kind of war, then, could be -- what type of war they were opting for? Could you please answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Obviously, the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina can be bloody and disastrous affecting all the three ethnic and three dominant religious communities. Depending on the status of the politician and his realistic influence on the political life in Bosnia and Herzegovina, they could carry certain clout, of course, if these words were the words of politicians who did not have political force following and support from the people from the grassroots behind them, that would not be recorded in the media or have any specific gravity. But if this was uttered by politicians in parliament, all politicians from parties in power that at any rate did have a very grave political weight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you a following question: A war, you could understand war to be military domination of a territory. Was there any clear view on whether it would be that or whether there would be any specific consequences for the civilian population in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the moment that we were talking about the gravity of the political situation was discussed only in official institutions and in some of the media by serious columnists who were analysing the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina, namely, we still did not have the necessary critical mass that could actually go to war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but that's not an answer to my question, at least not ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have understood, Your Honour, your question but I tried to be very precise in answering about the situation at that particular moment. At that particular moment, there were no military forces that could be the participants of a war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if there is a war option, I take it that you use violent means to achieve your aims. Would that aim just be military domination of an area or would that have specific consequences for the civilian population in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If that happened, it would certainly be military domination of a part of Bosnia and Herzegovina which would certainly entail consequences for the overall population, whatever part of Bosnia and Herzegovina that may be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, any military domination has consequences for the civilian population, but the question was whether it would have any specific consequences for the civilian population more than ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because of the heterogeneity of the population in Bosnia and Herzegovina, any war option would lead to the grouping of the respective three national or religious communities with their own sides. And ipso facto those who did not belong to any such communities would be jeopardised in certain parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So these beginnings of an ethnic division, any case leads to a war would have led to a war that would have catastrophic consequences for the population there. This is exactly what I talked about in my article from 1991, namely, if we did not grasp the reality in the field, homogenisation would be the deliverance of some and it would be reason for a revolt for others and therefore, we had to invest great efforts to understand this entire situation and leave it behind us as painlessly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say grouping of the respective three national or religious communities, grouping, that is, is that -- should I understand that as relocating them in accordance with the ethnically-drawn Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. lines?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just in relation to that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, I would just like to have the witness answer this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm talking about the initial stage, I'm talking about the political rallying which was actually making the other population segments uneasy. So I'm talking about this initial stage, the political rallying around the certain party which was actually to carry out in practice what the community in question agreed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said war option would lead to grouping. I was asking you what you understood by grouping. So we are not talking about political strife anymore, but we are now talking about the war option and what you meant by grouping. And I asked you whether that would include moving parts of the population.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite possibly as part of these political -- some of the political plans, relocating the population could be and would be an alternative, but I was actually also thinking about the more extreme solutions, the possible killing of the population, relocation, resettlement, even though it is a very serious international violation still leaves one alive, so there would be a mix of this resettlement and killing of people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be all the foreseeable consequences of choosing the war option; is that a correct understanding of your ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. Just in relation to this, of course, I realise that it's in view of the hybrid system that's adopted here, that objections against questions by Judges are not normally made, but nevertheless, I think it's appropriate because of the system that I come from where objections are made to Judges's questions, that I do make a marker there in relation to the leading nature of the questions on a question of such importance in relation to the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for putting your marker. Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, were there populations -- my apologies, I'll start again. Dr. Djokanovic, were there politicians who were advocating the separation of populations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frankly speaking, the entire ruling elite in that period was in favour of separation of the population, some explicitly and some implicitly. When I say implicitly, I'm talking about the Bosnian Muslims who expected to gain something with -- as part of this ethnic division but incidentally, let me mention also this: When the conference Yugoslavia started on the 14th of February, 1992, and of course I know about it only from the media, the three parties agreed to divide Bosnia and Herzegovina according to the territorial principle. The Croatian side said right at the beginning that they were sovereign over 17 per cent of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that they would not renounce their 17 per cent. The representative of the Muslim side, Alija Izetbegovic, said that the Muslims were sovereign and constituted in Bosnia and Herzegovina and were the most numerous people and it was out of the question for them to get less than one-third of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the representative of the Serbian side said that according to the land registry books, the Serbs owned over 70 per cent of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were the --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any case, all the three sides agreed at the very beginning about the percentile division of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were the ruling elite in the Bosnian Serb leadership?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just first --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just in terms of "ruling elite".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask the following. The witness used the words "ruling elite" on page 26 and now it disappears from my screen, but I have another screen. When you said "Frankly speaking the entire ruling elite in that period was in favour of separation of the population," did you have in mind the ruling elite of all parties: Muslim, Croats, Serb, or did you have in mind one specific part? I understood it to be -- to include all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the three players in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, if you use exactly the same words in your next question and add to it Bosnian Serb, then it could lead to confusion. Does this resolve the matter, Ms. Loukas?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that certainly resolves the matter to my satisfaction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, when you referred to the ruling elite --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you referred to the ruling elite, in regards to the Bosnian Serb leadership, who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the three ruling elites comprise national functionaries of the Assembly of the government, plus the functionaries of the ruling parties. Therefore, within the party infrastructure, the president of the executive Board, president of the executive board of the party, the main part officials.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In March 1992, who were the real decision makers in the leadership of the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I object to the general nature of that question. And again, terms like "real decision makers," in my submission, is very unlikely to be useful to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the word "real" suggests already something, that is, that those who formally were expected to make decisions would not be the real decision makers, at least that's the suggestion implied. On the other hand, the witness was in the position that he can answer the question who were the decision makers and could add anything as to formal positions and informal positions. So who were the decision makers in the, I would say, on the Bosnian Serb political scene?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer, Your Honours, in the sense of who were the leaders of all the three parties, I mean the decision makers and then in that context I would also respond in relation to the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that's a matter of fact that you answered the question in general terms, that political elite you would be consider to be party officials. Well, you mentioned a couple of categories of peoples. Now, the question specifically is: In view of the Bosnian Serbs and perhaps later on, someone will ask you about the Bosnian Croats or the Bosnian Muslims, but now specifically the Bosnian Serbs, who were the ones who were decision makers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that point in time, Dr. Radovan Karadzic was the -- undoubtedly, the main decision maker. Then members of the Presidency, Professor Koljevic and Professor Plavsic and the fourth decision maker at that time was Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, fourth influence was Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, in early 1991 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, what does it mean where the fourth person was it -- if you take the hierarchy, what do you mean by fourth in position? You have told -- you have given us certain names and behind this fourth person was there a fifth one, was the fourth person the last person on a list of four people? Was this the fourth people on the list of 20 people and why do you tell us that it's the fourth person? I'm sorry, but I could not really understand what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My reply was actually a reply in relation to both your dilemmas, both in hierarchy as someone who signed the appointments for members of the Presidency, Professor Koljevic, Ms. Plavsic and as someone who had signed the nomination for Mr. Krajisnik at the parliamentary elections, someone like that would be a very important political figure. Mr. Koljevic and Ms. Plavsic who got most votes for the parliamentary elections, thanks to their education, their social standing in the town and particularly because of their election results were undoubtedly ranked third. I wouldn't actually distinguish between the second and the third place in ranking. Mr. Krajisnik, as president of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, by his very function is distinguished from the deputies and becomes more important than the deputies, but the fact that -- because he received fewer votes at the elections, then Professor Koljevic and Ms. Plavsic, he could not be ranked equal with him. This was something that was taken into consideration to a large extent while setting up the Serbian state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to know if after Mr. Krajisnik there was another person who was influential -- how many influence people were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Except for the establishment of the Assembly of the Serbian people, there were no significant decisions and the Assembly of the Serbian People was established almost unanimously, there wasn't somebody taking a vote on it, it was a joint position of all the participants in this process at the time. Now after Mr. Krajisnik, there were the Serbian members of the government within the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina but they did not carry as much clout as to be ranked at this imaginary -- on this imaginary ladder of influence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I haven't finished. So the political influence was in the hands of four people; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The political influence of the people who constituted the ruling nomenclature of the Serbian people was wielded by these four persons whereas there were other people who carried clout, political clout, locally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the political influence of these four persons equal?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you make the question more specific, please? What period do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In early 1992.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The greatest influence was wielded, of course, by Dr. Karadzic. Next to him or after him, Professor Koljevic, Dr. Plavsic and Mr. Krajisnik. I wouldn't be able to be more specific than I've been in my last answer and I'm referring now to this period where we've been looking at the Assembly sessions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In early 1991, did you have a conversation with Dr. Koljevic about Momcilo Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You were asking me something that I indicated in -- that I've already indicated in my testimony. One day, during these Assembly sessions, we'd usually meet in Mr. Krajisnik's office because they seemed to be most appropriate for such meetings and Dr. Koljevic and I resided in the same part of the town and we usually took a walk at the close of these meetings on our way home. It was on this occasion that I told Professor Koljevic the following: Professor, does it seem to you that Mr. Krajisnik is struggling for more power than he'd actually need as President of the Assembly? That was something that I had already stated in my testimony. This struggle of his for a better position within the hierarchy of the Bosnian Serbs did not take him much higher than I've specified in terms of his ranking earlier on in May -- in March 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the war started, did Dr. Koljevic refer to that conversation you had with him and make a comment to you about that topic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About a year after this conversation of ours in Sarajevo, Mr. Koljevic said something unexpected. I must tell you first that when I told Mr. Koljevic what I've already said, he replied, Well, Dragan, I'm not sure about this. Where did you get this from? But then as we were walking once along Pale, he unexpectedly told me, Dragan, you were right when you stated that thing about Krajisnik. That's exactly how he told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the answers to Judge Hanoteau's questions, you referred to the deputies and the leadership of the Bosnian Serbs. Was there any one of the leaders who controlled, more than others, in the leadership, the deputies?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to that question. Firstly, that implies -- there's been no foundation for that question, and it's also a leading question. So in those circumstances, Your Honour, it should be rephrased so that whatever evidence there is to be elicited can be elicited in a less leading fashion. I particularly refer to this question of control more than others in the leadership. It implies, Your Honour, that there was such control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, would you please rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, in your response to Judge Hanoteau's inquiry about the level of influence of persons in the leadership of the Bosnian Serbs, you referred to four people. Now, those four people, you've told us were the leaders of the Bosnian Serbs. Can you tell me, out of those four people, whether any of them had more or less influence over the deputies?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor is very insistent so I'll have to give a wider answer. When we were at the conference in Belgrade on the 2nd of January, one evening Dr. Karadzic and I discussed the political situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina and at one point Dr. Karadzic says that there was fierce fighting going on for the second position. The second position in the hierarchy in the political infrastructure of the Bosnian Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina, this second in rank was supposed to belong to Mr. Krajisnik and then to Mr. -- but also to Professor Koljevic and Ms. Plavsic because they had received most votes for their position, whereas Mr. Krajisnik received these votes. And additionally, the votes first for him as a deputy and then votes for him as the President of the Assembly which gave him, following the elections for the President of the Assembly, in realistic terms, a very influential position in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, can I stop you there?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'd submit the witness should be allowed to finish his answer. Mr. Margetts asked the question and the witness should be allowed to give his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djokanovic, when you said that following the elections for the president of the Assembly, in realistic terms, a very influential position in Bosnia and Herzegovina, could you expand on that, on the position and the influence from that position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By inertia from the communist regime, we inherited a certain legacy where the President of the Assembly, this function was second most important position in the state. This is still true for our country which is in its in inchoate democracy stage, where it is not just a representative function as it is in democracies but it has great political influence even in the election of a government and especially within one's own party. May I continue answering the question put to me by the Prosecutor? However, Mr. Karadzic enjoyed enormous support by the people, those who were elected, Mr. Koljevic, Ms. Plavsic and Mr. Krajisnik knew that Mr. Karadzic's position was sacrosanct in the eyes of the Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina but also for Mr. Milosevic. This was the period when the Bosnian Serbs in Bosnia looked upon Mr. Milosevic as the most important politician for them and as a trustworthy person. So when we are talking about Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Karadzic is the most influential person. Next in rank are members of the Presidency and President of the Assembly. This is the position that I claim was such until the outbreak of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you're talking about the influence, you're very often using the word "the president was influential, the president of the assembly was influential." The word influence, would you please explain what you mean by that word. Is that a hierarchial power that they have over deputies? Is this a moral influential, is it an intellectual influence? Could you please explain to us what it means exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I use the term influence, I precisely meant influence on others because in our region, election results are still abused because those participating in the elections do not have specific differentiated political programs that they could present to the people. And then following the elections, work on implementing that program in association with the constitution and the laws. We still have this struggle for power over people so that the period we are discussing exactly entails this power and influence over people, even over deputies, yes, and even over ministers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And did that power, that influence, where does it come from? Does it stem from the title that one has acquired as a President of the Assembly? Is it due to the number of friends one can have or the network of friends? Is it due to a intellectual and moral dimension of the person? Is it because a person is extremely powerful and intelligent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the ignorance and the mediocrity of those who accept that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One additional question to you. You said about the influence of the President of the Assembly and you told us how that works in your region. Would this, what you said, would that be true for Mr. Krajisnik in that position or did he have the influence, as you told a President of the Assembly would have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would separate my own view -- my view in terms of two stages in the activities of Mr. Krajisnik, the stage when he was the president of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the stage when he was the President of the Assembly of Republika Srpska because the differences are substantial. As the president of the Assembly of Republika Srpska, he was exceptionally, exceptionally influential. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: ... the terms as you described, including influence on others, including deputies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm mindful of the time. Would this be an appropriate ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it certainly would. We will have a break until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, before I allow you to continue, I'd like to announce to the parties that I signed this morning a decision by this Chamber granting the request for a certificate for an appeal on the decision on the second motion for adjournment.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, from the start of the war until 20 April 1992, were you in the Vrace police headquarters in Novo Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is -- no, the house of my parents is in the immediate vicinity there and I used to live there with my family and I worked in the school that I referred to earlier in the infirmary, in the clinic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the 20th of April, 1992 until the 10th of June, 1992, were you in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the stated period, I was in Belgrade, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just prior to the 10th of June, did Professor Koljevic come to Belgrade and meet with you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he make a request of you, and if so, how did you respond to that request?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Professor Koljevic invited me to come to Pale and he relayed to me Dr. Karadzic's position, namely one of his utterances which was that he was actually wondering why I wasn't coming to Pale. So Professor Koljevic and I agreed that I should go there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Professor Koljevic mention to you any specific assignment you may have upon your arrival in Pale?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that day when we met, we -- actually the day before that, we discussed the situation in the field and then the next day we went to the SFRY Presidency to see Mr. Kostic. We also went to the building of the Serbian Presidency to see Mr. Milosevic. We also saw the patriarch, Pavle, in the patriarchate and I believe he also met with McKenzie during that day and later that day we flew together to Pale aboard a helicopter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went to Pale with Professor Koljevic, for what reason and for what task were you going to Pale to perform?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The day before when we had more time and during the flight in the helicopter, we talked about my possible involvement and how that would look at Pale. So Professor Koljevic told me in what state they at Pale were at that time and he told me that in force was a decision on the setting up of ^cap? War Presidencies [Realtime transcript read in error: "Commissions"] of the Srpska Republika, but that it wasn't being carried out in practice as they desired and that they were encountering major problems in the field. So talking about this, we tried to actually come up with an idea -- actually it was left more to me to come up with an idea of how to improve that particular activity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just check whether the transcription is right. Did I hear war presidencies for war commissions from the translators? The interpreters ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I did say War Commissions. I should have said War Presidency. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, as a matter of fact, I thought that I heard war presidencies and that it's either the translation or the transcription. I'm not blaming anyone but I'm glad that the matter that is been resolved. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, in light of Judge Orie's observance of the difference between War Presidencies and War Commissions, can you explain whether there was a difference between those two bodies?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived at Pale, there had only been in existence the decision on the establishment of a War Presidency which wasn't being carried out in practice so then I drafted the text on the creation on War Commissions and the idea was to establish communication between the municipalities and the Presidency at Pale all with a view to restoring their operation, the civilian organs of their authority so the Republika Srpska could actually be -- live as such in the field, through such municipal authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Could we have right now an explanation as to what exactly these War Presidencies are, what their role was, who constituted them, whether these were some kind of administration or could it be one single person, et cetera? I would like a detailed explanation of these War Presidencies and their particular functions. At the same time, I'm sure the Prosecutor is about to ask you about what those War Presidencies were, as to their role, et cetera. I would like a detailed explanation on this point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So when I arrived at Pale, the decision I had found there a decision had been published in the official gazette on the setting up of War Presidencies. I cannot recall the exact text of the decision but essentially what it was was that the previous Crisis Staffs were to be redubbed War Presidencies, I don't know whether comprising all the members or a reduced number. I cannot recall the exact decision because it was being carried out in practice. It didn't seem interesting enough for me to remember it. So knowing of such a situation in the field, aware of the situation in the field, I tried to draft a new text so that we could actually arrive at our ultimate objective. The ultimate objective being for the civilian organs of authority to become operational again and I'm talking about the deputies who were elected at the democratic elections in 1990. They were supposed to assume all responsibility for the situation in the field and of course do their job until the next elections. So that was the set objective. I drafted this decision on the establishment of War Commissions, no longer presidencies but commissions of trustworthy people to be designated by the republican commissioner together with the people in the field and to be verified by a corresponding member from the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Thereby we established direct liaison between the republican commissioner and the Presidency. And the commissioner would of course be operative in the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was that what you expected to do? Was that your role, how [as interpreted] to be fulfilled when you were requested to work within the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually I was the one who gave the idea about the War Commission and drafted the text and I submitted it to Dr. Karadzic who only revised parts of the text. My proposal was for the republican commissioner to appoint municipal commissioners so that this new body which thus emerged in the territory of the municipality would then convene a session of the municipal assembly calling the deputies elected in 1990 so that these deputies, after that constituent session, would actually elect the organs of authority and the new president of the municipal assembly. Karadzic did not accept this suggestion of mine, but actually thought that the municipal commission should comprise the president of the board of the SDS, deputy, a people's deputy, renowned citizen and the renowned businessman. I accepted it but I didn't think at the time, nor do I think now that it was a good move. I think that my suggestion was better than having the republican authorities formed -- that it was better to follow my suggestion to have the republican authorities formed with people who were not involved in the previous work on the Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask one additional question. You said the final aim was to make the civilian organs of authority to become operational again and you were talking about the organs as democratically elected in 1990. Was that a realistic option? This Chamber has heard quite some evidence on large numbers of either minority or majority populations leaving the territories of the municipality sometimes after having signed that they would give up all their property, sometimes with instructions published that if they would not report within a short period of time, they lost the right of residence. Therefore, it could be that large numbers of especially non-Serb members of the population were not present anymore on the territory. What was the -- to what extent was it realistic to restore on the basis of the democratic elections in 1990, the authority of the civilian organs and them becoming operational again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of the municipalities in which I was, it was only in Banja Luka that we had a similar situation as prior to the war. With the municipal Assemblies still multi-ethnic. In these other municipalities, these were mostly Serbian deputies, not for the most part, only, only Serbian deputies were comprising these assemblies. Although very flawed, still it was a much better variant than the chaotic situation that we had before that, at least in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not -- you said in other municipalities, these were mostly Serbian deputies. We were heard evidence on quite a number of municipalities where these Serbian deputies, municipal deputies were either a majority or a minority or almost equal. Did you consider it possible to restore these -- I would say these 1990 situation, democratically-elected Assemblies where the population had been -- well, was not in the same place anymore as it was before? Not, perhaps, the whole of the population, but at least we heard some evidence about parts of the population being moved. I'm not saying which part of the population but at least not living in the same place anymore as they did before. How did you imagine this to happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I hadn't expected that the entire municipal parliament would be able to become operational again. As I said, in Banja Luka -- actually applauded the efforts of the Banja Luka authorities and the Banja Luka politicians for their municipal parliament to be multi-ethnic. They invited me to Banja Luka although I was not directly entrusted by the Presidency to form the municipal orders of authority in Banja Luka but knowing of their desire to restore the 1990 elected organs of authority to operation, I did come to that assembly and I applauded their decision on behalf of the Presidency of the Serbian republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In these municipalities where I was as the republican commissioner, these were uninational assemblies comprising deputies in 1990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were they uninational assemblies in 1990 or was the remainder of the Assembly uninational comprising those who had been from that nationality that had been elected in 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the 1990 election, in the majority of municipalities of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were no mono-national assemblies. I don't know if that was the case anywhere, but -- because in most parts they were heterogeneous assemblies with a mixed composition with Serbian deputies in the majority in some parts, and Muslim deputies in others, and of course Croat deputies in parts where the population was Croatian in the majority. So with the exception of some municipalities in western Herzegovina where the population was mostly Croatian, this was the case, generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was there any -- apart from Banja Luka, you -- Banja Luka was an exception for the Republika Srpska territory? Yes. And any of the other -- in any of the other municipalities, was there real effort to restore assemblies as they were before the war started or was it just further developing the civilian authority of the Assembly as it was constituted after the war had started, which is mono-national or uninational, as you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not aware of there having been any efforts in other parts to constitute a multi-ethnic municipal Assembly and I'm speaking of the territory of Republika Srpska. Perhaps there may have been some efforts, but then I was not aware of them except for this example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers. Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could introduce now, Exhibit P527 which is the book of maps. It's not on the exhibit list and we could have one of the pages, and that's the page that Ms. Philpott has opened, placed on the ELMO which is page 20364-6506. Now, if the map could be moved over on the ELMO so that the eastern side of the map of Bosnia is shown. That's perfect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, on around the 12th of June, did you leave Pale and did you travel to the municipalities in which you had been appointed a War Commissioner?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you first, for the Court, outline which municipalities, as at 12 June, you were responsible for by indicating on the map with the pointer which municipalities they were and where they are situated in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Pointing is best done on the ELMO, Mr. Djokanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could start with the municipality of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm pointing at Vlasenica, then Sekovici, Zvornik, Bratunac, and Skelani. The Serbian municipality of Skelani, that's a part of the pre-war municipality of Srebrenica. In the summer of 1992, in August, I was also a commissioner for the municipality of Novo Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Possibly if we could then turn to the map of the Sarajevo area which is on page 25. Dr. Djokanovic, if you could just again indicate with the pointer the municipality of Novo Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the municipality of Novo Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Djokanovic. We won't be needing the maps any further. Dr. Djokanovic, could you just describe to the Court the trip that you made to this area and who you met with, what you discussed with them, and what you observed as you travelled around this territory?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the municipalities enumerated here, as the first municipality that I entered, starting out from Pale was Vlasenica. I dropped by at the building of the municipal assembly of Vlasenica but having found no one there, I went over to the municipal police building where I found the duty officer, Mr. Djeric. I didn't know him from before but he knew me so he knew who had showed up at the door. I told him what my purpose of the visit in Vlasenica was and he helped me get in touch with some of the people, members of the municipal authorities whom I met an hour or two later and I informed them of the purpose of my visit to Vlasenica. I showed them three documents that I had on me. One of them was a political platform concerning this activity. The second document was my appointment as commissioner of Republika Srpska and the third document was a decision establishing War Commissions. Because we didn't have much time, we didn't wait for the decision to be published in the official gazette. I, rather, went out in the field and we agreed that once I had toured the municipalities and I told them which municipalities I was going to go to, that they were to prepare a list of four people who were to man the municipal commission, whereas I was to be the fifth member of the commission. I told them that we were going to finish the process very quickly because they had all the papers telling them what they were supposed to do. After Vlasenica, I went to Sekovici where I had worked early on so I decided to spend the night there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, if I could just stop you there, was it the 12th of June that you were in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was either the 11th or the 12th of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
