utterances.text: Can you please describe to the Trial Chamber what you observed when you were in the city of Vlasenica in terms of the people you observed and anything that was notable about that city or different from how that city had been on the previous time you had visited?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vlasenica is a small town in Bosnia and Herzegovina with mixed population, and prior to the war, people were milling about the town, it was squirming with people because there was a bus station in the centre of the town. Now when I came to Vlasenica in wartime, Vlasenica was desolated. There's a road coming down from Mount Romanija right into the main street of Vlasenica which leads to the municipal building which is on the left side of the road. As I was taking this main street through the centre of Vlasenica, I saw a couple of uniformed people and there was none of the usual hustle and bustle in the town. It was quite empty as an inhabited area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you observe any civilians in the city of Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall seeing any civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any conversation with Mane Djeric or Milenko Stanic as to what had happened to the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not discuss this issue at all. We only talked about the issues surrounding the establishment of War Commissions and the consequential objectives. I spent very little time in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of the Susica camp that was located in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I didn't. Later on, of course, I heard about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you first hear of the Susica camp?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of the name Susica when I was following the trial of the commander Janke Nikolic but I remember that in the end of 1992, the president of Republika Srpska, Dr. Karadzic asked me to go to Vlasenica and tell the local people there that this camp, he called it, Logor, was supposed to be disbanded and he said it in a tone implying, Are they in their right mind? What sort of a camp are they holding there at the end of the 20th century. I went there because it was not far away from Pale and I conveyed this message to them. And I know that it was later on disbanded but I don't know the circumstances surrounding it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So after you visited Vlasenica, you mentioned that you moved on to Sekovici and am I correct that following Sekovici, you moved to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, after Sekovici, I went to Zvornik. On my way to Zvornik --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me for interrupting you, Mr. Margetts. I have a couple of questions before we look into Vlasenica. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Did you go thereupon instructions? Did you receive any orders to go there or did you go there spontaneously?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When Karadzic had signed the decision on the establishment of War Commissions, it was up to me to decide when I was going to set out on my journey. There was no concrete specific conversation between us on this issue. I made my own decision as to when to head on my journey and we had the documents which told us what we were supposed to do. We had the document establishing War Commissions. We had the document where I was appointed the republican commissioner so that in addition to the drafting of the text, there was no special communication about that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After you went to Vlasenica or on any other trip, were you supposed to report, I use the word "report", were you supposed to report on what you had done during your visit and any other visit you have might have done afterwards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My intention was to tour several municipalities. Upon my return to Pale, I submitted a verbal report. I was not required to submit a written report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last point. To come back to your visit to Vlasenica, you said this was a city in which there were not many people left, or at least there was no hustle and bustle, no people dressed in very different ways, different attire. And you said, well, I didn't ask any questions. Does that mean you were totally indifferent? You didn't notice much or if you did, that you ask any questions and just went about to carry on with your work? Can you give us -- can you enlighten us on this particular point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the period prior to my arrival in Pale, I spent a month and a half in Belgrade. My wife's parents lived at Zvornik in this period when the war broke out and we all got reunited because my wife and our children left Sarajevo and went to Belgrade where we all met and we -- I conveyed them my impressions about Zvornik and we had heard from the media that many people had left Zvornik and they themselves told me as they were leaving Zvornik, it was basically empty. That's how I saw Vlasenica as well, I simply thought that everybody had left and I did not specifically discuss this with the municipal authorities. I had to leave very soon and I expected that there was to go to be an opportunity at some of the later municipal meetings to discuss it. I did not really have occasion to discuss this matter with anyone during my stay in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what were your conclusions? What kind of interpretation of the facts did you give? I mean, the people hadn't just disappeared into thin air, had they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's very hard for me to remember what I was thinking about as I was driving from Vlasenica to Sekovici. On this particular issue you would like to hear my opinion about -- I really did not give it much thought. I only started thinking about it after Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, in Vlasenica, did the Serbian Crisis Staff -- had they established authority over the Vlasenica territory?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, just in relation to that question, I do object. If Mr. Margetts wants to elicit evidence of this sort then he can ask an open question as opposed to a leading one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any dispute about who established authority at that time in Vlasenica, Ms. Loukas?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm not happy with the evidence being elicited in this fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I did put a question to you, whether it's in dispute?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, there's no time frame on this question. It's too broad and general a question and any answer to that question would necessarily be unhelpful to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As far as the time frame is concerned, I did understand the question to be about the time of your visit to Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was not clear from the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was clear from the context, Ms. Loukas. Could you tell us who was having the authority, if any, at Vlasenica when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Without any doubt, Vlasenica was run by the Serb authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Serb authority was who, a municipal assembly, party organs from whatever party, Crisis Staff? What did you consider to be the Serb authority at that moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I entered the municipal building, it was empty. When I entered the police building, the chief of police was there in the main office who was a Serb. When I met with the municipal officials, when we entered the municipal assembly building, these officials were Serbs. I did not know these people from before and didn't know what their functions were prior to the war, whether they were functionaries of the municipal assembly; however, I know for a fact that all those who spoke to me that afternoon were Serbs. Perhaps -- I suppose they were officials of the SDS although I'm not sure about that either because I never asked them about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has heard some evidence about the creation and existence of Crisis Staffs, was there any Crisis Staff in Vlasenica at that time? You're nodding yes or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, they told me that there was a Crisis Staff in Vlasenica. Djeric and Stanic told me at that meeting. I told them that Crisis Staffs were ceasing operation and that we had to form a War Commission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... members of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can remember, all those people were members of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you arrive in Zvornik on the 13th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you meet when you arrived in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zvornik is a municipality in which I used to work before and I am quite familiar with it so that already at the exit of Sekovici municipality, at a crossroads, Sekovici/Tuzla/Zvornik, I could already see demolished and burnt-down houses and this is the first time that I saw such burnt-down houses. When I arrived in Zvornik, I could see on the other side of the bridge old people crossing over to old Zvornik, Stari Zvornik. These were predominantly old people and elderly women in the typical Muslim pantaloons, dimije. So then I walked over to the municipal building on the other side, entered it. I do not remember who was at the gate, but they told me that the Crisis Staff was in session in the municipal building and I actually barged in at this meeting in the -- of the Crisis Staff in the municipal building of Zvornik municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say you barged in can you describe to the Court how you entered and what you said, if anything?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said, at the entry gate, they told me that the session of the Crisis Staff was going on and that if I wanted to talk to anyone, I would have to go to that office where the meeting was. So when I opened the door, they were having this session, most of the people there knew me by sight as a doctor from the time before the war. Some of the people there, I, myself, knew, and I didn't know others and then I introduced myself and I stated my business. They adjourned the meeting of the Crisis Staff and there I had some consultations of the type I had in Vlasenica. I told them that it was my obligation to also tour some other municipalities, Bratunac and Skelani, for example, and they were to prepare a list of names of people to enter the War Commission and that we would talk in more detail on my way back because Vlasenica, Sekovici, and Zvornik were en route to my final destination which was Skelani. So on my way back from Skelani, I would be taking the same route to Pale and I could devote more time to all the details in the Zvornik, Sekovici, Vlasenica municipalities. Then I went to Bratunac, finished my business there regarding the commission, and on my way back, I talked at some length to the people in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that first meeting in Zvornik, who was present in that Crisis Staff meeting; can you name the people?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember seeing Brana Grujic, Jovo Mijatovic, the people's deputy, the president of the executive board of the SDS who we mentioned yesterday, Jovo Ivanovic. I also saw the then secretary of the municipality Stevo Radic. I also remember seeing a businessman from this community, Slavo Tomasovic and a couple of other people that I cannot recall but I can remember the faces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You informed the Court that you discussed the reason for your visit there and the setting up of the War Commissions, did you discuss anything else with any of those people at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time on that day, I did not discuss any other issues. We talked about these things when I returned from Skelani, when I returned to Zvornik going back from Skelani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On what date was that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was either the 15th or the 16th of June or possibly it could have been both the 15th and the 16th of June because I did stay the night in Zvornik so probably I saw these people on both the 15th and 16th of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Accepting that it was the 15th of June, on that occasion, who did you meet with?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked to Jovo Mijatovic, Jovo Ivanovic, Branko Peric, and I also talked with Brano Grujic but not on the 15th. After all, it was on that afternoon of the 12th of June, prior to my departure for Bratunac, and I'm concentrating hard here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you discussed -- when you had the conversation with Brano Grujic on the 12th or possibly the 13th of June, taking into account your earlier dating of your first appearance in Zvornik, what did you discuss with Brano Grujic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On arrival at this office where the Crisis Staff was, I realised that actually Brano Grujic was in full control of the situation. I stated my business to all of them, and then I said to Brano Grujic, whom I knew from before, because in 1991, I was once a guest at the Assembly of the Serbian Democratic Party to which he had invited me so we knew each other from then. And I asked him, Brano, why are all these elderly people leaving across the bridge from Zvornik to Novi Zvornik? Are you aware men of this -- what this looks like? And you can imagine if it looks like that way to me, how it looks like to the foreign press and what they can write about what is happening in Zvornik because elderly people never leave their residences. Do not let yourselves be accused of war crimes one day after the war is finished. But this remained a subject for future conversation, this impression of mine about how elderly people were leaving Zvornik across the old bridge to Mali Zvornik, so this was an impression which remained for future discussion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Brano Grujic the head of the Zvornik Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Again, I object to leading, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us who the head of the Zvornik Crisis Staff was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I stated in my reply that it was my impression that Brano Grujic was actually in full control of the situation. Who was formerly the president of the Crisis Staff was something that I didn't know. It was only later that I realised that Brano Grujic had been -- was, in fact, the President of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, you've described these elderly women dressed in Muslim clothing leaving the municipality across the bridge. What else did you observe in respect of the population of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was on my return when I arrived in Zvornik again when I met some people and stayed for some time in Zvornik. I could see that it was no longer the city in which I used to work and live once -- that it was more or less deserted, that there were a couple -- a handful of Serb returnees there, a handful of elderly Muslims in the city. They told me, I think, that there was still some Muslims in Divic which is a suburb of Zvornik and that there was some Muslims downstream the Drina River in Kozluk. So I talked to my acquaintances, people that I knew from before and this is what they told me. It was -- I was given quite a few bits of information by these people and armed with that information, I came to my renewed talk with the leaders of the Zvornik municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say they told you there was some Muslims in Divic and there was some Muslims in Kozluk, when you were a doctor in Zvornik, were there Muslims in other areas of Zvornik as well as those other cities?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I think that the Zvornik municipality area had 80.000 inhabitants in all of which 50.000 were Muslims. I believe that the town proper had about 17.000 people with all the suburbs that is. I believe that the majority there were also Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from the Muslims in Divic and Kozluk, where were the other Muslims?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These elderly people were mostly in the towns -- in -- sorry, houses in the periphery in the outskirts of the Zvornik town. I don't know about the situation in either the surrounding Muslim or Serbian villages, I -- I'm just talking about the town proper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the town proper, did you meet with any Muslims?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not meet with any Muslims. In fact, I did meet one woman Muslim, Mila Puskarevic. Her husband was a refugee in Belgrade and she was also supposed to leave for Belgrade those days and be reunited with her family. She worked with handicapped children so she stayed on for a while to work with such children there. So I inquired after some people, talking to her, I asked about her brother Mustafic who was a physical education teacher, a good friend of mine, who had, in fact, called me to come and work in Zvornik and it was on his account that I had come to work in Zvornik. He was a very enthusiastic athlete and had a very good sports chapter in Zvornik. So I also ask about some other people whom I had known and she had told me that they had left and departed Zvornik. Also I talked with an elderly person from Zvornik, a good friend of mine, Slavko Dragutinovic, an old man who was very familiar with the circumstances and people in Zvornik. At a certain point in time, he told me, Doctor, help us, we cannot go out in the street. Not only have they driven away the Muslims, but now they are threatening us as well. There are groups of armed people going up and down the streets and you never know whose house they will barge into. I also heard about my friend -- an old friend of mine Muhamed Jelikic, that he had been let go, but I believe that he had paid for it, either in money or that he had given his house for being let go. And I also heard that Dr. Jelikic cried before Marko Pavlovic for this guy to let him go and be reunited with his family. Dr. Jelikic otherwise has two daughters, one of whom is in Serbia. Sorry, married to is Serb, is married to a Serb, correction. So I was really emotionally charged and when I saw all these people again in this municipality, they were not -- it was not really a nice experience for them to talk to me because I told them -- I asked them whether they were at all aware that this war would end one day. All wars in history ended so that one would have to end one day. I asked them whether they were aware that there was some documents accompanying this war, documents which the International Community adopted after the Second World War in relation to Nazi Germany and they were still in force. Perhaps they were a bit frightened at that moment, and they told me that they, too, were intimidated by these paramilitary units that were there. Then I asked them, What kind of government are you? You have a full hotel of the police, you have mobilised the entire reserve police force, what do you think they are doing? What do you think you are doing? So they remained speechless, in a word, to what I had said to them. In fact, I don't think they liked my story at all, although at that moment, it was only meant to warn them but it was very well meant. It was only well meant. I did not actually categorise them as people who would be able to inflict any harm on anyone, rather, I thought that they were people who were not up to the task of actually responding to the gravity of the moment. They were all amateur politicians without any previous political experience who failed to comprehend the fact that political office also entailed the responsibility, not only privileges. And it was in a bad mood that I left Zvornik and passed through Sekovici and took this paper in Sekovici -- also in Vlasenica, I talked for a while with Professor Lukic, an elderly man ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You referred to the conversation you had in Zvornik after you had been informed by an acquaintance, among other things, that the Muslims had been driven away and you referred to "them," as the people you were talking to. Can you name the people that you were talking to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned Milan Puskarevic, Slavko Dragutinovic. I was also in the health centre with the colleagues that I used to work for before. It is hard for me to remember the names of the people and to say exactly who it was that I talked to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I meant when you spoke to the Serbian representatives in Zvornik, who were you speaking to at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I returned from Bratunac and Skelani I talked to Jovo Mijatovic and Jovo Ivanovic and Branko Peric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also meet with the leadership of Zvornik on the 30th of June and the 1st of July?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that period, we had a meeting between the leaderships of Skelani, Zvornik, Bratunac, Vlasenica, and Sekovici in the Zvornik municipal assembly building. It was Dr. Karadzic, Ratko Mladic and I who came to this meeting from Pale and it was the first official political delegation that went out into the field, at least it was as recorded as such by a newspaper published by the news agency Srna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also meet with the leadership of Zvornik on the 19th of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 19th of August, a constituent session of the Zvornik municipality was held and I attended that session. I was -- I found myself in a highly unpleasant situation. Someone had prepared a fierce campaign, even a smear campaign that had started ever since the session was opened. There was the introductory speech by Mr. Grujic, the people who were cooperative, Jovo Ivanovic and Jovo Mijatovic with who one could really communicate and talk to. That Branko Grujic, or rather, his father-in-law had gone to the lobby with the deputies who were on the battlefield to be elected president of the Zvornik municipality, Municipal Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Assembly and who was slinging mud at me. I endured this or deal and I even tried to ignore or at least leave an impression of ignoring these statements of theirs and then I took the floor and I told them what I really thought of what they had been doing in Zvornik. I told them that I was a representative of the Serbian Republic, that I was a commissioner of the Presidency, that I was a commissioner of their government, their Assembly, and that finally, I was a commissioner there on behalf of the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina -- of the Serbian republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I familiarised them with the results of the plebescite, told them that the Serbs had chosen to stay in Yugoslavia but the Serbian people did not say that they wanted to remain alone in Yugoslavia, that nobody had the right to do something that might harm the Serbian people in the future and that the Serbian people were never genocidal or criminal in their history and that all those who had committed crimes would be brought to justice one day. There were various unpleasant comments levelled at me from the conference hall. But I remained in the conference hall throughout the session where the Zvornik Municipal Assembly was elected. Brano Grujic was elected the president of the Assembly and upon my return to Pale, I briefed them about it, I told them that the Assembly was constituted and that everyone was doing in accordance with the decision on the appointment of commissioners but I told Professor Koljevic and Dr. Karadzic all about the ordeal that I was exposed to during my stay in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask you a question, Witness. To go back to this visit that took place, you said on the 15th or on the 16th of June, am I mistaken? It took place on the 15th and on the 16th of June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It must have been on the 16th of June that I was in Zvornik. The municipalities of Bratunac and Skelani are very near to each other and I believe that I returned from Bratunac to Zvornik to spend the night there and then from Bratunac to Skelani and then on the 16th, I returned to Zvornik so that I'm certain, 100 per cent, that I spent both the 15th and the 16th in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to make sure that I understood you correctly. Is it the first time that you were able to notice physically the effects of a policy you talked about, burnt houses, destroyed houses. You talked about a population of elderly people who were leaving towards Serbia. Was it the first time that physically you were noticing the effects of it all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I experienced the beginning of the war in Sarajevo. In the part where I lived at Vrace, there were no such things to be seen. Next, I went to Belgrade to work as the president of the coordinating body and I received invitations from many embassies of many countries that wanted, after the convention of Yugoslavia, and after the letter that I had sent to all the accredited diplomats in Belgrade asking them to use their offices with their governments to make sure that Yugoslavia is preserved and that one day the citizens of Yugoslavia would be grateful to them for it. However, this -- in this period, many ambassadors were revoked from Belgrade so that I was not able to visit all those that I had wanted to visit. However, I was very much occupied and busy with all -- with this business and my wife and children were in Belgrade as well, but we did not have a TV set at home so I was unable to follow what was going on in Bosnia and Herzegovina and in that part specifically. So I was unaware of the goings on on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When was it the first time that you were able to notice there on the field that things were happening.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I was at Pale, Pale functioned as a multi-ethnic community, Muslims lived there without any problems until a tragedy occurred in Zepa. So we who lived in Pale did not see much of what was going on in the field. I understand, Your Honour, what your question is, but I keep telling you what I -- I keep telling you what I actually saw. I cannot tell you that I heard something different because I was unable to follow the mass media, when I was in Belgrade and when I was at Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm terribly sorry for being so stubborn, but my question is the following: On the 15th of June, when you arrived in Zvornik, is it the first time that you noticed, yourself, that you saw with your own eyes, burnt houses, destroyed houses, and people who seemed fleeing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. So could you please tell us what was your reaction personally? How did you feel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that in my earlier answer, I tried to describe vividly how I felt and what mood I was in when I left Zvornik. There is nothing I could add to my previous answer. In my case, I felt defeated in -- to tell you, specifically, when I was heading out of Zvornik. It was a town that I had worked in, where I had organised the meeting with Karadzic and Zulfikarpasic. In order to make this town an example of a town where people decided to live together, especially because it borders with Serbia, and besides, I had some emotional links with the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How did you feel when you saw people leaving, what was your personal inner feeling at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was in June 1992 and now it's 2005 and I still have an image of the old bridge before my eyes. Can you picture an old lady hardly walking and she's fleeing. Why is she fleeing? I don't think she really feels like living very much anyway. Why would she be crossing the bridge? There's nothing more that I could tell you on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you told us, therefore, that you were very emotional?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That same energy brought me here to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, precisely, I was wondering, on that day of the 15th of June, you went and you met members of the Crisis Staff, Jovo Mijatovic and Jovo Ivanovic, you saw them. What did you tell them? Did you tell them, as I understood earlier, "Be careful, the reporters are here. You might be convicted." Is that all you told them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps the best thing would be to present a document here. When I was attacked by the Serbian Assembly in 1993, to look at a reaction by one of the deputies and I'd kindly ask the Prosecutor if they could see to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Answer my question, sir. You were facing these two members of the Crisis Staff, what exactly did you tell them? You were standing there in front of them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours asked me any more questions on that matter further -- how I had experienced this and how I reacted at a politician [Simultaneous English and French interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm listening now to the French and the B/C/S and I'm waiting for a confirmation that the French translation functions again.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness repeat his answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said Your Honours, please do not ask me to describe further that which I had already tried to describe with words. As a politician, I had already spoken on this matter and was the only one in the region to have spoken on that matter despite the risks and since that moment, my life has changed completely. Ever since, I had no peace any longer. I did not have any permanent place of residence. I did not have a secure job, a steady job. My reaction at the time was such that at one of the regional meetings in Bijeljina, Brano Grujic stated, "The Muslim president and a Serbian functionary accused me of being a war criminal. When in 1993 I warned Dr. Karadzic about the turning point in the Serb policy at the Assembly meeting there, I then went through something that a person of my physique probably would be unable to endure. Once again, I urge the Prosecutor to present here a comment by the national deputy, the then president of the executive board of the SDS, Jovo Mijatovic at the Assembly session in 1993. By your leave, Your Honours, I believe that this would help to round off this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And one more question, Witness. The people from the Crisis Staff, do you think that they could have stopped what took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they could have at least tried.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How could they have done that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just talking now about these old people whom I saw and about that particular issue. They could have visited them every day and if they could have entrusted some younger people in the municipality, if we accept, as a hypothesis, that people left Zvornik, had left Zvornik fearing the war, the Crisis Staff people could have charged some of the municipal servants with visiting these old people every day. This is what I told them: "Take them some medicaments every day. Take them some bread every day. You could then tell the foreign journalists, the people have fled, the population has fled. But look, we are looking after those who remained. You have old people fleeing their houses and fleeing to Serbia even though they don't like Serbia, but they are fleeing to Serbia because they feel safer there. Any day on the morrow you may be accused of genocide." So sentence of mine was later abused, politically abused. Or when you say you may be accused or the other variant is "they may accuse." In our language that can mean either "they may accuse you" or "I may accuse you." So it depends on the actual emphasis or the stress that you place on the word. It can mean either. So I really couldn't do anything but what I actually did given the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since you've spent a day and a half in Zvornik, were you able to find out who were the authors of these destroyed houses, who had caused all those damages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The houses that I referred to on the outskirts of Zvornik municipality, I really don't know who burned those. But as for the town proper, it wasn't really damaged. There were no ruins inside the city. As for who did these other things, they told me at that moment, that this was done by these paramilitary groups that were on a rampage in Zvornik and that no one could actually hold in check. That is why I asked them, "Well, what are you doing with your police? You have the Zvornik police, the Zvornik brigade. You have your army." Apart from that warning, I also wanted to bring the leaders of the Serbian republic to Zvornik, Dr. Karadzic and Mladic. And they responded. They were at this meeting in Zvornik attended by the representatives of all these municipalities. So I brought to that meeting these leading people, the meeting of the leading municipal people. I brought to them the top civilian man and the top army man to attend their meeting to discuss all the different various topics. When I arrived at Pale, I did tell them about everything that was going on in the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I have but one last question for you, sir. You said in your statement when you were talking about the Crisis Staff, you used the word "amateurs," could you elaborate on that? Could you tell us why did you call these people amateurs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A professional politician, you see, especially one elected by the people, would abide by what he had offered to the people. The parties that want power in Bosnia and Herzegovina had offered their programmes to the people. Those were quite acceptable political programmes. And all those who remember well 1990 know that I supported the existence of national parties in Bosnia and Herzegovina because their programmes did not actually indicate that what later happened would happen. Their programmes spoke about democracy, the protection of human rights, personal security, the security of property. The professional politician who wins the elections will remember why he won the elections. But these were frauds. These were cheats. In no programme of any political party starting from Slovenia to Macedonia in 1990 will you find anything -- will you not find the sentence that they were advocating the preservation of Yugoslavia. In all of them, they say that they will respect international governments and charters on human rights and all the Geneva Conventions. Every programme will say that they will guarantee personal security. Not in a single programme you will see that they are not guaranteeing the safety of property. But if this is in the programmes and you deviate from all of that, then you are no longer a professional, you are an amateur and you are a bad man. Those are bad people. What were their motives to engage in politics in the first place? Why did they want to be in power at all? What did they want to do with power if they didn't -- if they wanted ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... War.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, we are close to the break. I don't know if you have any further questions on the issue you started more than 20 minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, we do have some further questions on that matter so we're happy to break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not necessarily at this moment. If you say -- if you think you could deal with them in the next three minutes then fine; if not, then we could either have an early break or I could put an additional question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: If you'd like to, Your Honour, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm trying to fully understand your position at that time. You did not tell these people you committed war crimes and you will be held responsible for that. You said, "Please beware that the one who commit war crimes can be held responsible for it." Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you had observed, did that give you the impression that war crimes had been committed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It gave me the impression that war crimes had indeed been committed there in that area. I could not have been more direct. In fact, knowing my own self, this was not -- it was not by chance that I said this sentence which I told them, "You may be accused of war crimes." However, I did not have reliable information. I did not have any substantive proof of individuals having participated in such dealings to be able to say that at Pale. And people, in fact, avoided talking about the subject. In the next period, the prime minister of the Serbian Republic, the first prime minister, Djeric, several days after I had returned to Pale, at Jahorina, in fact, in this building called Kikinda where I was with Koljevic and Plavsic and where in fact the government was, so we were walking in front of this building with Djeric and he told me, "You have regards from Zvornik. They are sending their greetings, these people from Zvornik. They like you." Not knowing who he was referring to, I said, "Yes, of course, I worked there previously. I know lots of people there." And then I noticed that he meant one thing and I was saying another. Then several days after that when we saw each other at Pale, when he talked to me about my involvement in the government --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you because you give quite a wide answer and I might be interested perhaps in other details as come to your mind. So you said that what you observed gave you the impression that war crimes, indeed, had been committed. You were hesitant to directly confront the persons you were speaking with about responsibility since you had insufficient information that they were the ones responsible; is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't hesitant, I was very explicit talking at Pale about the situation that I had found in the field. I could not speak on an individual basis, because I didn't know who the people were who could have done that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you don't mind, there might be some confusion. You did not say directly to those you spoke with in Zvornik, "You are responsible for the war crimes I see that have been committed here," because you had insufficient information to accuse your partners in this conversation; is that correct? You couldn't say, "You, Mr. X, with whom I'm speaking at this moment, you're responsible for these war crimes." Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, maybe with hindsight, with all the knowledge that I have now, I would have been more direct then because after all, I'm a medical person by profession. So reading the charters of the World Health Organisation and other charters and international documents, I knew these things and would have warned those people. But I did perhaps say more than I actually knew about. I said to Brano Grujic, "Who is going to return to Zvornik? What kind of a Zvornik are you talking about? Look at yourselves. Look at your city. What kind of return of people are you talking about? The elderly are leaving. Who is going to come to that kind of a town, to that kind of a Zvornik?" I couldn't say specifically about anyone getting killed or by any specific person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that you saw war crimes that had been committed, you couldn't say to the one you spoke with, "You are responsible for this killing or you are responsible for that destruction." And therefore you, gave it a more general form saying that, "If you commit war crimes, you may be held responsible at later stages." Is that -- do I understand it correct, that you gave it that form?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I told them, "You are the government. You are responsible. Your names will stay on paper. War crimes do not fall under the statute of limitations. One day you will be held accountable. I don't know who the main culprit is but as they do not lapse, one day someone will be held accountable." And this is what I said at the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes but I'm at this moment, I'm interested in what you told the people in Zvornik during this meeting. Let's go to the -- you told me that you -- from your observations, you concluded that war crimes had been committed by whomever and you warned that this could lead to being held responsible for that. Did you report to Pale, later on, that on the basis of your observations, that you concluded that war crimes had been committed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. There was nothing unclear there. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To whom did you report that exactly, apart from ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 16th in the afternoon on my return, all the members of the Presidency were there. First, I met Biljana Plavsic at the entrance to the building, and I told her immediately about everything that had transpired in the field, and later also to Professor Koljevic, and Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you don't report ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, the interpreter hasn't finished.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I'm also not sure whether I also told Djeric that evening when he returned from the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you reported on the basis of what you had seen, the conclusion should be that war crimes had been committed. Did you specify what type of war crimes or did you give them -- I mean war crimes is a very general qualification, isn't it. There could be many varieties of it. Did you specify in whatever way on the basis of your observations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I told them that people in the field were telling me that many ugly things had happened, that many crimes had happened in the field. I don't think that even now I'm able to give you a legal differentiation in terms of how this should be characterised under international law, but as a human being, I can tell you that people were killed, they were driven away from their houses, and that this happened on a massive scale and this is what I found out from talking to people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's what you told the members of the Presidency upon your return to Pale, that people were killed and driven out on a mass scale and that was the information you got; is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you have understood me precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were your own observations either supportive or non-supportive of what people had told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I saw was a confirmation. I never doubted for a moment that the stories that the people were telling me in Zvornik were untrue because these are serious people and people whom I trusted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And are you certain about the presence of the members of the Presidency? You expressed some doubt about the presence of Mr. Djeric, but do you have any doubt as to whether you told Ms. Plavsic, as you said, Mr. Karadzic, professor, what's his name again, Koljevic, and Mr. Krajisnik, do you have any doubt as ... I see you're nodding no. For the transcript, that doesn't appear but I understand your answer to be in the negative. We'll adjourn until 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the parties will have one second, please, for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour, there's just a matter I need to place on the record at some point prior to the witness recommencing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One second, Ms. Loukas. I was informed that -- the interpreters informed me that on page 30, close to line -- in line 11, after the word "hierarchy" that the name was mentioned by the witness, the name Karadzic, and that although that appears from the rest of his answer, it is something that should be put on the record. There's another matter I would like to address and it's mainly for you, Mr. Margetts. The Chamber is aware that we took over questioning of the witness for almost half an hour in totality. It is not the intention of the Chamber to interfere at such a scale with the examination by the parties. At the same time, perhaps you may have noticed that the Chamber, and this relates also to what I said yesterday, that apart from exploring all the other political options that would have existed or would have been in the mind of whoever -- so apart from exploring that in much detail, that the Chamber very much is inclined to find -- to find the information which sometimes seems to disappear in a lot of words which not always have the clarity one would wish if one is seeking to establish what actually happened. That's what I'd like to say. I have another very technical matter which is not related to this witness, but Ms. Loukas, I'll first like to give you an opportunity to make the submission you'd like to make.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour will recall that earlier this morning, I placed a marker down in relation to questions from Your Honour. I will place a similar marker down in relation to the series of questions from Your Honour just prior to the break. Of course these are in circumstances where we are in a hybrid system and judges do ask questions and it's not the done thing here other than in exceptional circumstances to object, although, of course, coming from a common law background, it's somewhat different in my system. But leaving that aside, Your Honour, I would submit that the series of questions Your Honour asked just prior to the break do constitute such an exceptional circumstance and I do make this submission in the interest of justice and that is this: Leading questions in evidence in chief are of course particularly for matters that go to the core of the case are always objectionable, Your Honour. And the basic philosophy behind it, of course, is that the evidence must come from the witness, not from the questions of the questioner. But in my submission here, the situation is much more serious, a fortiori, Your Honour, when the questions come from the Bench, when such leading questions emerge from a Judge, the temptation for a person in the witness' position to agree is too great a danger and is not in the interests of justice. And in my respectful submission, Your Honours, evidence of that nature that goes to the core of the case should not be elicited by a judge in a leading form, and I place that on the record, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Ms. Loukas. I will consider since, of course, you address not only the Chamber but me as -- not only as Presiding Judge but also as the Judge who has put some questions to the witness, I will consider whether I ask any further specification as to the lines, et cetera, because one thing should be certain, that is, that I want to take every observation by any party with the seriousness it deserves.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I much appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I move to the other issue, that is I have to raise it now. Mr. Djokanovic, it will not take much time. I ask for your patience. On the 11th of March, Mr. Harmon, a motion for protective measures for three witnesses were filed, witnesses to appear soon, according at least to the schedule and I know that the schedule is not certain anymore, but there are two questions in relation to those witnesses. First, according to the second revised list of witnesses which was filed on the 4th of December, 2003, these three witnesses appear to have a pseudonym already assigned to them in another case. The motion does not mention this fact and therefore, our interpretation of the table of the 4th of December might be a wrong one. We'd like you to clarify this by tomorrow whether, at least, protective measures were already assigned to these witnesses in other cases. Second, the motion was filed on the 11th of March. Looking at the Rule 126 bis, the Defence has 14 days for a response. That would have been, because the last day to respond would be a holiday, then finally, it would be the 29th of March which would be the last day for filing a response. But the witnesses, of course, were apparently already due to testify next week and therefore, I'd like to hear from the Defence whether there's any problem in responding to the motion by next Monday, that's the 21st of March, even if it will be orally.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll look into that when the Court finishes today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm fairly sanguine that we can meet that timetable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Loukas, for that cooperative attitude. Mr. Margetts, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, in addressing the members of the Crisis Staff of Zvornik, you stated to them that any day they may be accused of genocide. Why did you utilise the word "genocide"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look at the population in Zvornik. If the oldest of residence leave Zvornik, if things occurred for which one knows with certainty are crimes today, even the President of the Crisis Staff stated that a little genocide, as he put it, had been committed in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your discussions with the President of the Crisis Staff, Brano Grujic, did he use those words that you have just used, that is, that "a little genocide occurred in Zvornik"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, he did not use these words in his conversation with me. This was later written about in the papers. But he never publicly denied having said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your understanding of the term "genocide"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking of me to give you a definition of this term or do you want me to speak of Zvornik? Because if you're asking me to give you a legal definition, then I must tell you that I'm not a law student.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, in terms of your use of the word, when you used it, what did you mean?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I use the term only as a person involved in politics. If an area is cleansed of members of another ethnicity, of another religious community not to leave any trace that, then this would be a definition of genocide, as far as my legal knowledge goes, and as far as my political convictions go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was it that -- was it your understanding that's what had occurred in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's always better to ask, what was your understanding or what was your specific knowledge of what had occurred in Zvornik as opposed to, was it your understanding that that's what had occurred in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts. Would you adopt this as a better phrasing in a more open question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Not in this instance, Your Honour. The use of the word Zvornik was in reference to the events -- the use of the word "genocide" was in reference to the events in Zvornik and so it seems to me that this question flows from the evidence that's been given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just reread.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you allow me. In other words, what I'm saying is, you have now provided a more specific and detailed explanation to the Court as to what you meant when you used the word "genocide" with reference to Zvornik. Does that specific explanation apply to what you observed in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, if phrased this way.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If phrased this way, would your objection still stand?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: If Mr. Margetts is rephrasing the question, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As he did. He's more or less giving -- so perhaps, Mr. Margetts, put the question in the words you last used, that is: Mr. Djokanovic, you have provided a more specific and detailed explanation to us as to what you meant when you used the word "genocide" with reference to Zvornik. Is that specific explanation, does that apply to what you observed in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The only remaining resident of Zvornik from before the war who was a Muslim and who changed his name subsequently was a guard at the cinema. He had two sons and his children played with my children for the period when we lived in Zvornik. One of the children's names is Milos. When I asked him, son, what's your name, he replied Osman Bravo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not directly an answer to the question put to you first in rephrasing by Mr. Margetts and now by me. That explanation that you gave about the word "genocide," is that specific explanation -- does that apply to what you observed in Zvornik? I didn't hear your answer and perhaps the interpreters didn't hear either.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, you mentioned that Brano Grujic said that a little genocide had occurred. Can you tell the Court precisely what Brano Grujic said in regard to this little genocide and that is the context of his comments?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just in relation to that, the evidence given by the witness was not that Brano Grujic had said this to the witness, but that it was in the newspapers. That was the evidence that was given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, as far as the -- to the extent you reflect the evidence, could you do it with the highest precision, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, you've heard the interjection of my learned friend. Insofar as you either read in the newspaper or otherwise heard that Brano Grujic had said that a little genocide had occurred, can you please tell us exactly what Brano Grujic said?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, I've already said what Brano Grujic said as far as I remember. In addition to the conversation we had during the war, I can only mention him in one, another example when I came to the office in Zvornik. This was something in relation to the humanitarian relations and there was a person present there and he approached me and said that he apologised for all the accusations that he levelled at me at the beginning of the war. And I can't tell you more than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, I'd now like to leave Zvornik and your work as a War Commissioner and take you back to Pale. When you arrived in Pale on the 10th of June, which building did you go to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I was leaving Pale in the direction of Jahorina, there's a building on the right-hand side owned by a company from Kikinda Vojvodina prior to the war, so they called it the Kikinda building. That's where the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was housed. We were there, the Presidency was there until it was moved to the new premises near the Panorama Hotel at Pale.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: At the Panorama Hotel in Pale.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived in Pale, who constituted the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Presidency included Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Koljevic, Ms. Plavsic, Mr. Krajisnik, and the Prime Minister Djeric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the date that you arrived on the 10th of June, how many Presidency sessions did you attend?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except for the period when I was in the field in late June, I was present at the Kikinda building daily. We would start working early in the morning and then finish working late in the night, depending on the matters worked on. We would work more intensely in the afternoon hours but would start usually working at around 10.00 in the morning. That's when we would meet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So apart from the period from the 12th of June to the 16th of June, during June of 1992, you were meeting with the Presidency each day?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except for the periods when I was in the field. But when I was at Pale, I was normally at the Kikinda building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe to the Court how these meetings were conducted, that is, how the Presidency functioned?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said, we would start working at 9.00, 10.00 a.m. and then continue working until late in the evening. The working hours were not formalised, that is, the beginning and the end of the sessions were not formalised. There was a relaxed atmosphere but we worked throughout the day. As far as I can remember, Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik had their diaries where they took note of what was discussed. I believe the same was done by Professor Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In which offices in Kikinda did you meet?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you enter the building on the ground floor, there is a restaurant with a conference room. And then as you go on the first floor, you had the bedrooms where we slept and on the right-hand side, you had offices. To the left, also, there were two offices where the secretaries were and the office of Mr. Krajisnik, President of the Assembly. And the last room to the left was a room where we used to work, sometimes we'd have lunch or dinner there. Just ahead of this particular room, there were the office of Biljana Plavsic and Mr. Koljevic and there was also a room where I worked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In which room did you meet with the Presidency members?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, in the room behind the rooms where the secretaries were, where Mr. Krajisnik worked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you mean Mr. Krajisnik's office?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that, of course, is leading and I object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's a point of clarification only in the room where Mr. Krajisnik worked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: To me, I think it invites the next question for purposes of clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, what's the difference between a room you work in and your office? Usually -- I'm not saying that I'm never working out of my office, but what's the difference?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, how about just in whose office did you meet?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: "In whose office did you meet?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but the previous answer was: "In room did you meet? "For the most part in the room behind the rooms where the secretaries were, where Mr. Krajisnik worked."

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Whose office was that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the room. Behind the room. So it's the room where Mr. Krajisnik worked. That's not his office?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Whose room was that, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What do you mean by whose room was that? Let me just then read carefully through. "Which room?" was the question at 84: 7. "For the most part in the room behind the rooms where the secretaries were, where Mr. Krajisnik worked. I understand this to be in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the room where Mr. Krajisnik worked.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed Your Honour, but all I'm saying is the next question could be in whose room was that, as opposed to the question that Mr. Margetts asked. Mr. Margetts has a constant habit of leading, and Your Honour, it's not acceptable in relation to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Ms. Loukas also you could say the next question should be Was that room specifically used by one or more persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or you could have done -- and then of course, we reach a point where the objection against this kind of leading is not making much sense anymore.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I maintain my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Your objection is denied. At the same time, Mr. Margetts, to the extent possible, it would have taken you just as much words. And knowing how sensitive the issue is for the Defence, I advise you to phrase your questions in such a way that there's no need to object and there's no need to give a ruling on the objection. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, in which room did Momcilo Krajisnik work?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Krajisnik was sitting in exactly this room which I referred to earlier. There were no markings on it, on the door.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you describe that room as being anyone's office or did you not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the office in which Mr. Krajisnik usually sat, but there was nothing written on the door. It was an office with a working desk, a chair behind the desk, and a couple of chairs in front of the desk for whoever was talking to the person sitting behind the working desk, and that was Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the Presidency met, who chaired the meetings?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall a single session that was so formal as to have been chaired over by anyone and minutes kept. Usually, Mr. Krajisnik would be sitting behind his desk and we would be sitting at desks in front of that desk but we could also meet in this room which was to the right in the corridor where you didn't have a main, a head desk, as it were, but just a couple of chairs lining the walls. But if we talk in a formal way about the sessions, the sessions would be open by Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you consider were the ultimate decision makers in the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Undoubtedly these were Dr. Karadzic -- Mr. Krajisnik and Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the moment that you arrived in Pale, what was your impression as to the relative level of authority of Karadzic and Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, something happened in this period when I was in Belgrade after the month of March, that is, and the last Assembly when we had practically walked out of the building, when they had told us that there had been crimes committed in Sijekovac which is a place near Bosanski Brod where 10 or 13 Serbs had been killed. So when we received that bit of information, we abruptly left the conference hall, the Assembly room, and all of the Serbian leadership was at Pale in June. So some things had happened in that period. That is why I said that I divided Mr. Krajisnik's influence in two stages. The first stage being when he was the president of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the second when he was the President of the Assembly of Republika Srpska. He was really -- he really wielded a lot of authority and it was my impression that his clout equalled that of Dr. Karadzic, provided however that I could notice; but mind you, I do not know well either one of them that Mr. Krajisnik was always loyal to Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As the year 1992 progressed, what was your assessment of the authority that Krajisnik had over the deputies?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in relation to a question of this nature, I would submit that a general question of this nature is not of assistance to the Trial Chamber. If the witness is able to provide specific evidence about what he saw, heard, observed, that's one thing, but to ask a general impressionistic question of this nature, in my submission, is of no or negligible assistance to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, the assessment and the impressions the witness gained might not be without relevance but, at the same time, if we do not know on what those impressions are based or on what basis those impressions are made, it loses almost all if not everything of its weight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's our position on this that this was an individual that had access to both Karadzic and Krajisnik over a long period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: For certain purposes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: If I might interrupt at this point, it's probably not appropriate for the witness to have his headphones on during the discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not know whether -- Witness, do you understand any English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, if you would please take your earphones off for a second. I do understand -- you don't have to leave. I do understand, Mr. Margetts, that if you, during a long period of time observe the behaviour of certain persons, that it means that the assessment -- well, at least could have some value and some weight. At the same time, if it's not supported by any other evidence to be given by the witness, then of course it's just a personal opinion and of course witnesses are not here to express their personal opinions. If an opinion is part of the answer of the witness, then it should at least be clear that the opinion has some solid factual basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the factual basis that we've sought to establish is that association and that could be an explanation as to why there was a lengthy examination into the early parts of this gentleman's association with the leadership. Part of that examination included the evidence that when he was present in the vicinity, he was -- he attended each of the assembly sessions and that as someone that did attend all of those assembly sessions during 1992 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Margetts, but isn't it true that if you put two people in the same situation for a longer period of time and if you asked their opinion about what happened, that there might come up with totally different opinions and that the most important thing then is to find out on what exactly they've based their opinions and assessments. So the mere fact that you have been there for a longer period of time is certainly not sufficient to enable the Chamber to assess whether this opinion or whether this impression is a logically-understandable opinion or assessment based on what the witness has observed. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the witness could have his headphones replaced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, you've given evidence before this Chamber that you attended most of the Assembly sessions of 1992 and, in fact, we've produced notes from those Assembly sessions where you are the speaker following Mr. Krajisnik and, in fact, during the Assembly sessions, it's Mr. Krajisnik that's chairing those sessions. During the course of 1992, from your experience in the Assembly, did you gain any -- did you form any opinion as to which person in the Assembly had the most authority over the deputies?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Undoubtedly the most authority in the Assembly was that of Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you refer to this authority that Mr. Krajisnik had by any particular phrase?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That summer, I talked to some people at Pale, especially after the conversation with Dr. Koljevic, who said, and we referred to that today, "Dragan, you were right about Mr. Krajisnik." So there was some people and I talked to them and I said that in principle, there had been established in parliament an unregistered political party that was being headed by Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your function as a War Commissioner, who did you report to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In respect of municipalities, in principle, all the appointments of municipal commissioners would be signed by Dr. Karadzic as the President of the Presidency provided, however, that the direct tasks by the -- in the Presidency as regards the commissioners, that changed. It would be Karadzic and then it would be Krajisnik -- and then it would be Koljevic and then it could be also Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did those three individuals have authority over the commissioners at different times or did they have authority together during the entire period from the formation of the commissions?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to that question, just in relation to giving a witness two alternatives does not detract from the leading nature of that question and I would object to it on that basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your objection is sustained. Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, in June of 1992, who were the War Commissioners subordinate to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That being an initial stage in the work of the commissioners, Dr. Karadzic was the one who -- Dr. Karadzic having been the one who had signed the decision drafted by me and as I was, in principle, the first commissioner in this republican commission, I was the one who mainly cooperated with him regarding certain details. I think that later, Professor Koljevic was in charge of some municipalities and then later in the second half of July, I think, this particular task working with the municipal commissions within the Presidency was the task of Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your role as the Novo Sarajevo commissioner, who did you report to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Novo Sarajevo is my municipality and the delegation from Sarajevo was led by Branko Radan who was one of the municipal officials in that period. In fact I also spoke on television about the work of the municipal commission so that my activities were known as they had great problems to constitute the Municipal Assembly they came to me for me to come to Novo Sarajevo to help them transact that business. I said no problem, but Mr. Krajisnik is in charge of these activities, so if you agree with him, there is no problem. As far as I'm concerned, I will accept. Mr. Krajisnik had no objections. He accepted this. So I went to Sarajevo as the commissioner but with a decision to that effect signed by Mr. Karadzic anyway, because the commissioners were subordinate to the Presidency, but with the individual members having certain tasks in certain periods and Mr. Krajisnik was in charge of the work of the commissioners then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, I look at the clock. It's a quarter to 2.00. I take it that you have not finished yet your examination in chief or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, right on the bell, that concludes my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's -- being aware that at least for considerable time, the Judges have put questions to the witness, let's now see how we proceed. I do understand that you have no further witnesses for this week. That means, Ms. Loukas, that -- how much time would you need for cross-examination of the witness? Not to prepare, but first of all, let's establish on how much time approximately you would need.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour. As I indicated at the beginning of the week, there's quite some material I need to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
